summary: Jesus is handed to Pilate, who asks if he is King of the Jews and gets a non-answer, then falls silent altogether. Pilate can see the charge is driven by envy and tries to release him, but the crowd asks for Barabbas — an actual insurrectionist and killer — and calls for crucifixion. Soldiers dress Jesus in purple, crown him with thorns, and salute him as king before leading him out. He is crucified at nine in the morning between two robbers, mocked by everyone including the men dying beside him. At noon darkness falls; at three he cries out that God has abandoned him, and dies. The temple curtain tears, and the Roman officer in charge says he was the Son of God.
whyItMatters: This is where Mark's whole book lands. The title announced in 1:1 is confirmed by a human being for the first and only time in 15:39 — and the human is the enemy officer running the execution, who says it not because of a miracle but because of how the man died.

context.author: Anonymous; early tradition names Mark, recording Peter's preaching
context.audience: Readers in the Roman world who knew what crucifixion was — Mark uses Latin terms and names Simon's sons as if they were known to his community
context.setting: Jerusalem on the day before a Sabbath, during Passover; the Praetorium, then Golgotha outside the city wall
context.literaryForm: Passion narrative told with unusual restraint — Mark reports the physical facts of crucifixion in a handful of words and spends his detail on who says what

outline.heading: Before Pilate
outline.note: Two words, then silence — and Pilate is astonished by it

outline.heading: Barabbas
outline.note: The crowd chooses a man who actually did what Jesus is charged with

outline.heading: The soldiers' game
outline.note: Purple, thorns, a reed, mock homage from an entire cohort

outline.heading: Golgotha
outline.note: Simon of Cyrene compelled; the crucifixion in five words; three rounds of mockery

outline.heading: Darkness and death
outline.note: Noon to three; the cry in Aramaic; a loud shout, and it is over

outline.heading: The curtain and the centurion
outline.note: The temple veil torn top to bottom; the officer's verdict; the women who had followed from Galilee

outline.heading: Buried
outline.note: A council member risks himself to ask for the body; two women watch where it goes

keyVerses.text: “Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani?” which is, being interpreted, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”
keyVerses.why: The only words from the cross Mark records, and they are a cry of abandonment, preserved in the language he spoke.

keyVerses.text: The veil of the temple was torn in two from the top to the bottom.
keyVerses.why: Torn from the top — Mark specifies the direction, and it happens the moment he dies.

keyVerses.text: Truly this man was the Son of God!
keyVerses.why: The claim of 1:1, finally spoken by a human being — a Roman executioner, and the last person you would expect.

keyVerses.text: who, when he was in Galilee, followed him and served him
keyVerses.why: Mark waits until now to tell you the women had been there the whole time. They are still there, and the Twelve are not.

questions.question: Why does the case go to Pilate at all?
questions.answer: Because under Roman rule the council could try religious matters but apparently could not carry out a death sentence on its own authority — though scholars debate how far that jurisdiction actually reached (compare Stephen’s stoning in Acts 7). So the charge has to be translated into something Rome cares about, and it is: blasphemy becomes kingship. Notice that Pilate never asks about blasphemy — his one question is whether Jesus claims to be King of the Jews, which in a Roman province is sedition. Same man, different indictment, depending on which court he is standing in.

questions.question: Why does Jesus stay silent?
questions.answer: Mark makes a point of it — Pilate marvels at it, which is a strange thing to record about a prisoner. He answers the direct question about kingship with something closer to 'that is your word,' and then says nothing to the accusations. Isaiah 53:7 describes a servant who does not open his mouth before his accusers, and readers have long heard that here. Whatever else it is, it is a refusal to negotiate, and the contrast with the noise of everyone around him is the point.

questions.question: Was releasing a prisoner at the festival a real custom?
questions.answer: All four gospels mention it and no outside source records it, which is why some historians doubt it. Arguments for plausibility: Roman governors did have discretionary power to pardon, and gestures of goodwill during a volatile festival would have been shrewd management. It cannot be confirmed independently. What is worth noticing is what Mark does with it — a crowd chooses between two prisoners, and takes the one who actually led an armed uprising over the one accused of it.

questions.question: Is this crowd the same one that shouted Hosanna a few days earlier?
questions.answer: Mark does not say so, and the assumption is worth resisting. This is early morning at the governor's residence, a gathering the chief priests are actively working (verse 11 says they stirred them up), while the Galilean pilgrims who lined the road are elsewhere. The chapter is not a story about fickle public opinion so much as about a managed proceeding — Pilate wanting to please the crowd, and the crowd being steered.

questions.question: Why do the soldiers dress him in purple with thorns?
questions.answer: It is a mock coronation, and every element is a piece of costume: purple was the colour of royalty because the dye was ruinously expensive, the thorn crown parodies the radiate crowns on imperial coins, the reed is a mock sceptre, and 'Hail, King of the Jews' parodies the salute to Caesar. They are staging a joke. The irony Mark relies on is that they are also, without knowing it, staging the truth — and the sign nailed over his head says the same thing in earnest.

questions.question: Why name Simon of Cyrene's sons?
questions.answer: It is a striking detail — the man carrying the crossbeam is identified not by himself but as 'the father of Alexander and Rufus.' That only helps if the readers know who Alexander and Rufus are. It reads as a note for a specific community where those men were present or remembered, and Paul greets a Rufus in Romans 16:13. It is one of the small internal details that supports the tradition connecting this gospel with Rome.

questions.question: Mark describes the crucifixion itself in almost no words. Why?
questions.answer: Verse 24 says 'Crucifying him, they parted his garments among them' — the execution gets a participle and the soldiers' dice get the main clause. There is no description of nails or agony anywhere in the chapter. Two reasons are usually given. His readers had seen crucifixions and needed no explanation. And Mark's interest is elsewhere: he spends his words on who mocks, what they say, the darkness, the cry, the curtain, and the centurion. The restraint is a choice, and it is more effective than detail would have been.

questions.question: 'Save yourself and come down' — is that just cruelty, or is something else going on?
questions.answer: Both. Three groups mock in turn: passers-by, the chief priests, and the men crucified with him. But the taunt in verse 31 is accidentally the summary of the whole gospel — 'He saved others. He can't save himself.' They mean it as proof he is a fraud. Mark expects the reader to hear it as the exact truth, stated by people who have no idea what they are saying. It is the same technique as the mock coronation.

questions.question: What does the cry of abandonment mean? Was he actually forsaken?
questions.answer: This is among the most debated verses in the New Testament and honest readers differ. Some hold he genuinely bore separation from the Father in that moment, taking the weight of human sin. Others point out that the line is the opening verse of Psalm 22, that quoting a psalm's first line was a way of invoking the whole, and that Psalm 22 moves from abandonment to vindication and ends with God not despising the afflicted — so the cry carries its own answer. Others hold that both are true: the anguish is real and the psalm is deliberate. What no reading can soften is that Mark gives us no other words from the cross. This is what he chose to record.

questions.question: Why do bystanders think he is calling Elijah?
questions.answer: 'Eloi' and 'Elijah' sound close enough to be confused, especially shouted by a dying man. There was also a popular expectation that Elijah came to rescue the righteous in extremity. So the misunderstanding is natural, and Mark records it with a certain bleakness — even his last words are misheard, and someone suggests waiting to see if a rescue arrives. None does.

questions.question: What is the temple curtain, and why does it matter that it tore?
questions.answer: A heavy woven veil separating the innermost sanctuary — the Most Holy Place, which only the high priest entered, once a year — from the rest of the temple. It was the physical statement that access to God was restricted. Mark notes the direction: torn from the top to the bottom, which is to say not by human hands. Readers have taken it as the barrier removed, as judgment on the temple, or both. Either way, the moment it happens is the moment he dies, and it happens in a building on the other side of the city from Golgotha.

questions.question: Why is the centurion's line the climax?
questions.answer: Because of the shape of the whole book. The narrator says Son of God in 1:1, a voice from heaven says it at the baptism and the transfiguration, and demons say it repeatedly and are silenced. No human being manages it — Peter gets 'Christ' in 8:29 and immediately shows he does not understand it. Then the officer commanding the execution squad, a Gentile, watching a man die badly with no rescue and no sign, says it. And notice what triggers it: verse 39 says he saw how he cried out and breathed his last. Not a miracle. The death itself.

questions.question: Where are the disciples? And who are these women?
questions.answer: The disciples ran in 14:50 and have not come back — none of the Twelve is mentioned at the cross. The women were there, and Mark tells you only now that Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joses, and Salome had followed and provided for him since Galilee, along with many others who had come up to Jerusalem with him. They watch him die, they watch where he is buried, and they are the ones who come to the tomb. In a book about who stays and who understands, Mark's answer is delivered quietly, in a list, in the last chapter and a half.

questions.question: Who is Joseph of Arimathaea, and why was asking for the body risky?
questions.answer: Mark calls him a prominent council member — part of the same body that condemned Jesus — who was himself looking for God's kingdom. Crucified bodies were normally left to hang or thrown into a common grave; that was part of the punishment. Going to the governor to request the corpse of a man executed for claiming kingship identified him publicly with the condemned. Mark says he went boldly, which is a pointed word in a chapter where the men who promised to die alongside Jesus are nowhere in sight.

glossary.def: The governor's headquarters. Mark uses the Latin term, as he does 'cohort' — a unit of several hundred soldiers.
A prisoner held with insurrectionists who had committed murder. The name means, roughly, 'son of the father' — an irony most readers have noticed.
A Roman public execution reserved for slaves, rebels, and the lowest criminals, designed to be slow, exposed, and humiliating. Roman citizens were normally exempt from it.
Aramaic; Mark translates it as 'the place of a skull.' Outside the city wall, beside a road, so that passers-by could see.
Counted from sunrise: roughly 9 a.m., noon, and 3 p.m. Mark marks the day in three-hour intervals.
The curtain screening the Most Holy Place inside the temple, entered by the high priest once a year on the Day of Atonement.
A Roman officer commanding around eighty men. The one here is in charge of the execution detail, and gets the last word about who Jesus was.
